blocks.title: Honors — what does the slope MEAN?
blocks.markdown: On a velocity-time graph, the slope is the acceleration. CPA reads off the number. Honors defends what that number *is* — and refuses the common slip that confuses a high velocity with a high acceleration.

## Reading an a-t story from a v-t graph

The slope of a velocity-time graph is $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ — **how fast the velocity is changing**, not how fast the object is going.

- A **steep** v-t line claims large acceleration: velocity changing quickly.
- A **flat (horizontal)** v-t line claims **zero** acceleration — even if the object is moving fast. Constant velocity means no change, means no acceleration.
- A **negative** slope claims the object is slowing (or speeding up in the negative direction).

The honors trap to avoid: *'it's moving fast, so it's accelerating fast.'* Wrong. A spacecraft cruising at 10,000 m/s with a flat v-t line has **zero** acceleration. Speed lives on the axis; acceleration lives in the slope.

blocks.title: Common slip
blocks.markdown: *'High velocity means high acceleration.'* No. A high, **flat** v-t line is fast but unaccelerated. Acceleration is the *change*, the slope — not the height of the line.

blocks.frame: On this v-t graph the slope is ___, which means the acceleration is ___. A classmate who says the fast-moving object 'must be accelerating a lot' is wrong because ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY: Point to a segment of today's velocity-time graph and state what its slope means physically. Then refute a classmate who claims a fast-moving object on a flat v-t line is accelerating — explain what the flat slope actually tells you.
